title: MC2-08234
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The appellant is appealing the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his claim for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The appellant, XXXX XXXX XXXX, is a citizen of Tunisia.

Should he return to Tunisia, he fears for his life at the hands of XXXX XXXX (hereinafter referred to as "C."), a radical Islamist member of the Salafist political party Ennahdha, who attacked and threatened to kill the appellant for criticizing radical Islam.

The appellant is appealing the Refugee Protection Division (RPD) decision rejecting his claim for refugee protection. He submits that the RPD erred in its analysis of an internal flight alternative (IFA) in Sfax and Hammamet. He also asks the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) to accept new evidence.
For the reasons set out below, the RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct. An IFA is available to the appellant in Sfax and Hammamet.
The appeal is dismissed.
The appellant asks the RAD to accept the following new evidence that was not presented to the RPD: * Exhibit "A" - Statement of source deductions, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX2022.1

To be able to rely on evidence that was not presented to the RPD, the appellant must demonstrate to the RAD that this evidence is admissible under subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA) and the criteria in Raza,2 as adapted in Singh3 (Singh/Raza). Exhibit "A" is not admissible as evidence

The RAD concludes that the statement of deductions intended to show the information retained by the Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale [national social security fund] in Tunisia (Exhibit "A") does not meet any of the criteria in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA. Consequently, this document is not admissible as evidence.
The appellant submits that it is evidence that did not exist at the time of the RPD hearing.

The RAD rejects this argument. The RAD accepts that the statement in question was issued after the rejection of the claim by the RPD. However, the RAD is of the opinion that evidence to the effect that a taxpayer's address is information held by the Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale in Tunisia is information that was available before the RPD rejected the refugee protection claim. The appellant does not submit that this is a new procedure in Tunisia. Furthermore, he testified before the RPD that, if he were to return to Tunisia, he would have to work and, to do that, he would have to provide his address to the Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale.4

The appellant gave no explanation as to why documentary evidence corroborating his testimony could not have been provided to the RPD before the rejection of his refugee protection claim. Consequently, the RAD is of the opinion that he failed to demonstrate that this is information that was not reasonably available before the rejection of the refugee protection claim.

With regard to whether this is information that the appellant could reasonably have been expected to have presented to the RPD, the RAD considered that the IFA was a determinative issue at the hearing before the RPD. Furthermore, he was asked about Mr. XXXX ability to track him down in the proposed IFAs.
In light of the above, the RAD is of the opinion that the statement of deductions does not meet any of the criteria in subsection 110(4) of the IRPA.

In addition, the RAD is of the opinion that this is not new evidence. First, the appellant testified about this information before the RPD. Furthermore, the RPD did not doubt the appellant's testimony in this regard. Consequently, the new document cannot be used to contradict a finding of fact by the RPD.

That said, although the statement of deductions is not admissible as evidence, for the purposes of its analysis, considering the appellant's uncontradicted testimony in this regard, the RAD accepts that, if he were to return to Tunisia, he would have to provide his contact information to the Caisse nationale de sécurité sociale in order to be able to work. THE REFUGEE APPEAL DIVISION CANNOT HOLD AN ORAL HEARING
The appellant submits that he is presenting Exhibit "A" in support of a new hearing before the RAD.
However, under subsection 110(6) of the IRPA, the RAD may only hold an oral hearing when certain criteria are met, particularly when new evidence is admissible.
Considering the previous conclusion that Exhibit "A" is not admissible as evidence, the RAD cannot hold an oral hearing pursuant to subsection 110(6) of the IRPA.
The RAD applied the correctness standard of review.5 The RAD conducted an independent assessment of the evidence, including listening to the recording of the hearing.

In addition to his arguments regarding the IFA, which will be addressed below, the appellant also submits that the RPD erred by failing to conduct a separate analysis of the claim under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.
The RAD rejects this argument. In reading the RPD's reasons, the RAD notes that the RPD conducted an analysis of the claim under both section 96 of the IRPA and subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

However, like the RPD, the RAD concludes that the appellant has failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution on one of the five Convention grounds or, on a balance or probabilities, that he would be subjected personally to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, under subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, if he were to return to Tunisia. The Refugee Protection Division did not err in its analysis of an internal flight alternative in Sfax and Hammamet
The IFA determination is based on a two-pronged test.

For the first prong, refugee protection claimants must establish that there is a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA in the proposed IFAs.

For the second prong, refugee protection claimants must establish that it would be objectively unreasonable for them to seek refuge in the proposed IFAs. The appellant failed to establish that there is a prospective risk in Sfax and Hammamet

The RAD is of the opinion that the RPD did not err in concluding that the appellant had failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution in Sfax and Hammamet or, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be subjected personally to a risk there within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA.

The appellant submits that several of the conclusions or inferences drawn by the RPD are based more on assumptions and conjecture, rather than on clear conclusions based on the evidence. He adds that the RPD made a number of sweeping conclusions. He submits that the RPD minimized the role played, as well as C.'s motivation and ability to track him down in the proposed IFAs. He adds that since the RPD found him credible with respect to his allegations, he is also credible with respect to the lack of an IFA. He adds that the RPD erred by failing to address C.'s ability to track him down anywhere in Tunisia, through the information he has to disclose to social security.

The RAD disagrees with the appellant's arguments. It is incumbent on me to note that the appellant has the burden of establishing that his agent of persecution would have the interest and motivation to track him down in the proposed IFAs.6 However, like the RPD, the RAD is of the opinion that he failed to discharge this burden.

The appellant's testimony revealed that during his stay in Tunisia from XXXX 2014 to XXXX 2015, he met C. three times, always at the same café.7 Furthermore, according to the written statement of his friend XXXX, he also ran into C. in XXXX 2022, again at the same neighbourhood café.8 In the circumstances, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant failed to establish that these meetings with C. were anything more than chance encounters.

According to the appellant's testimony, C. lives in the same neighbourhood as his parents.9 The café where the altercations with C. occurred is about a ten-minute walk from the appellant's parent's home.10 However, according to the appellant's testimony, over the past eight years, neither his family nor his friends in the neighbourhood have been approached by C., other than the encounter with XXXX at the café in XXXX 2022.11 When asked by the RPD why he had not had any news from C. in all these years, the appellant stated that he did not know whether C. had tried to find him and that, furthermore, he is the one that C. has a problem with because he stood up to him.12

However, as noted by the RPD, the appellant's father and the appellant's two friends went to the police station with him. His friends were willing to testify against C. Nevertheless, the RAD accepts that C. would only be interested in the appellant and not his parents or friends. That said, they have never been approached by C. in all these years, other than a chance encounter with XXXX at the neighbourhood café in XXXX 2022, to find out the appellant's whereabouts. Yet, these individuals all live in the same neighbourhood near the café frequented by C. In these circumstances, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant has failed to establish that C. is actively looking for him or that he would have the interest or motivation to track him down in the proposed IFAs. In light of the evidence presented by the appellant, namely, that all the interactions with C. took place at the same neighbourhood café, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant has failed to establish that the risk he would face at the hands of C. would extend beyond the neighbourhood in question.

With regard to C.'s ability to find him in Sfax or Hammamet, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant failed to establish this. The RAD accepts that the appellant would have to disclose his contact information to social security if he were to return to Tunisia. At the RPD hearing, the appellant stated that since C. is a member of the Ennahdha political party, he could have access to his information.13 That said, as noted by the RPD, the appellant did not provide any evidence regarding C.'s role in that party or the influence he may have in the party. At the RPD hearing, the appellant admitted that he did not know what C.'s role was in the party and had not tried to find out about this role.14 Consequently, the RAD is of the opinion that the appellant has failed to establish that C. could have access to his personal information because of his membership in the Ennahdha political party. That said, even if C. was able to access such information, as previously stated, the appellant has failed to establish that C. has the motivation to take such steps to try to find him.

With regard to a risk at the hands of religious extremists in general because the appellant is a non-practising Muslim, the appellant does not contest the RPD's conclusion that he failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA on this basis. The RAD sees no error and agrees with this conclusion.

In light of the above, having considered all the evidence, the RAD concludes that the appellant has failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, a risk within the meaning of subsection 97(1) of the IRPA in Sfax or Hammamet. It is not unreasonable for the appellant to seek refuge in Sfax or Hammamet
The RAD is of the opinion that the RPD did not err in concluding that the appellant failed to establish that it would be unreasonable for him to seek refuge in Sfax or Hammamet.

Without any specific argument, the appellant cites case law stating that the IFA must be a realistic, attainable option, and the claimant cannot be required to encounter great physical danger or to undergo undue hardship in travelling there or in staying there.15
The threshold for showing that an IFA is unreasonable is very high. The conditions in the IFA must be such that the refugee protection claimant's life or safety would be at risk.16
At the RPD hearing, besides his fear of being found by C., the appellant stated that he would not experience any problems with settling in the proposed IFAs, and working and living there.17

The appellant is a young 31-year-old man who speaks French, English and Arabic.18 Arabic is the country's official language and French is used in commerce.19 The appellant has pursued university studies.20 In Canada, he has held various jobs in the XXXX XXXX industry,21 which he could also do in Tunisia.
Consequently, the RAD concludes that the appellant has failed to establish that he could not settle in Sfax or Hammamet, support himself, find accommodations and live there safely.

In light of the above, the RAD concludes that the RPD's decision is correct. The appellant has failed to establish a serious possibility of persecution on one of the five Convention grounds or, on a balance of probabilities, that he would be subjected personally to a danger of torture, to a risk to his life, or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, pursuant to subsection 97(1) of the IRPA, if he were to return to Tunisia.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the determination of the RPD that XXXX XXXX XXXX is not a "Convention refugee" under section 96 of the IRPA or a "person in need of protection" within the meaning of section 97 of the IRPA.
